> No one fail to understand this. My point is simple and that is you can make endless account with one email id

I think we all understood your point.

The problem is that you don't know how email provider `provider.example` handles its accounts. You *cannot*  say if `foo.bar@provider.example`, `foo+bar@provider.example`, `foo-bar@provider.example`, `foo_bar@provider.example`, `foo~bar@provider.example` (and even `foo💩bar@provider.example`) are the same user/mailbox or not.

Even *validating* an email address in the first place [is a mess and is often botched](https://www.netmeister.org/blog/email.html) resulting in people being blocked from registering accounts on some websites because their *valid* email addresses are considered invalid by the website's email validation logic.

Therefore you *cannot* implement such a rule without potentially breaking legitimate users (or worse, conflating two different emails addresses to the same account).

Anyway, even if you could do what you you propose without breaking legitimate users, it would be pointless anyway because:

1. creating a wide range of gmail emails accounts (or some other email provider) is not a big problem difficult anyway;
2. you can get your own domain name `superhacker.ovh` for around 3$/year, redirect *all* the emails addresses of this domain (`0000000000@superhacker.ovh`, …, `9999999999@superhacker.ovh`) which would allow you to create millions of accounts, bypassing your proposed security verification.

Now, you want to to prevent someone from creating a flock of bogus spam accounts in your application, you can:

* implement some rate limit (per IP address/block, etc.);
* implement from JavaScript/WebAssembly-based proof-of-work for each account creation;
* implement some CAPTCHA;
* any combination thereof.

(Note: Oh by the way, the left part is insensitive to `AAA@example` and `aaa@example` are expected to be the same address.)
